title: Trevithick's Iron Horse
summary: A tall, strong engineer from Cornwall called Richard Trevithick built steam engines small enough to move. In 1804 one of his engines pulled heavy iron wagons along a track in Wales, the first time a steam locomotive ever hauled a load on rails. It worked, but it was so heavy that it kept cracking the rails!

sections.heading: The Cornish Giant
paragraphs: Richard Trevithick was born on 13 April 1771 at Tregajorran, in the parish of Illogan, a scattering of cottages between the mining towns of Camborne and Redruth in Cornwall. His father, also called Richard, was a mine captain, which meant he managed the men and machines of a tin or copper mine. Young Richard grew up in a landscape of engine houses, spoil heaps and pumping beams, where the thud of Newcomen and Watt engines could be heard day and night.

At school he was not a star pupil. Teachers found him stubborn and easily bored, though he could do difficult sums in his head faster than they could on paper. What he really loved was the engines. As a teenager he followed his father around the mines, and by his early twenties he was working as an engineer himself, building and repairing pumping engines.

He also became a local legend for his size and strength. He stood about 6 feet 2 inches (about 1.88 metres) tall, very tall for his time, and Cornish people called him the 'Cornish Giant'. Many stories were told about him: that he could lift enormous weights, throw a sledgehammer clean over an engine house, or write his name on a beam high above his head. Some of these tales were surely improved in the telling, but everyone agreed he was powerful, fearless and full of restless energy.

In 1797 Trevithick married Jane Harvey, whose family ran Harvey's foundry at Hayle, one of the most important engine-building works in Cornwall. That same year he became engineer at Ding Dong mine, near Penzance. Working with another engineer, Edward Bull, he began to experiment with engines that worked differently from the Boulton and Watt design. Boulton and Watt suspected these engines broke their patent on the separate condenser, and they took legal action. An injunction, a court order telling him to stop, was even pinned up at the mine. For a few frustrating years, Trevithick had to be careful.

Then, in 1800, Watt's patent finally ran out. Trevithick was free. And he had already decided which way to go: not bigger, low-pressure engines like Watt's, but small, powerful engines working with high-pressure 'strong steam'.

sections.heading: The Puffers
paragraphs: As we saw in Part 3, a low-pressure engine needs a big cylinder and a condenser full of cold water. Trevithick threw the condenser away. His engines let steam into the cylinder at much higher pressure than the air around it, let it push the piston directly, and then simply blew the used steam out into the air. Each blast of exhaust made a loud 'puff', so these engines became known as 'puffers' or 'puffer engines'.

Getting rid of the condenser had big advantages. The engine no longer needed a huge supply of cooling water or a tall engine house with a giant beam. It could be built compactly, with the cylinder sunk right into the boiler to keep it hot. A puffer could be much smaller and lighter than a Watt engine of similar power, cheaper to build, and quicker to put up. In the Cornish mines, Trevithick's compact engines were soon used to wind ore and men up and down shafts.

In March 1802, Trevithick and his cousin Andrew Vivian took out a patent for high-pressure steam engines, including their use to drive carriages. Trevithick had grasped something that Watt never had: an engine light and strong enough to carry its own weight could move itself. And if it could move itself, it could pull other things too.

Trevithick was also very good at boilers, which were the dangerous part. He made cylindrical boilers of wrought iron, rounded so that pressure pressed evenly on the walls, and he placed the fire inside a tube that ran through the water, so that the hot gases heated water all around them. It was a big step toward the kind of boiler that later locomotives would use.

sections.heading: Christmas Eve on Camborne Hill
paragraphs: Picture Camborne on Christmas Eve, 1801. It is cold and dark, and the narrow street called Fore Street climbs steeply up Camborne Hill. Out of a workshop rumbles a machine no one in the town has ever seen: a boiler on wheels, glowing at the bottom, with a chimney belching smoke and sparks and a cylinder puffing out clouds of steam. Trevithick had built a full-size steam road vehicle. Local people nicknamed it the 'Puffing Devil'.

Andrew Vivian steered, and several men climbed aboard, around six by most accounts, with others perhaps hanging on wherever they could. With a great hissing and puffing, the Puffing Devil set off up Fore Street and up Camborne Hill towards the nearby village of Beacon. Climbing a steep hill with passengers on board was a real test of power, and the machine passed it. For the first time, people in Britain had travelled in a full-size vehicle driven by steam.
The excitement inspired a Cornish folk song, known as 'Camborne Hill', which people still sing today. It celebrates the day the steam carriage went up the hill, with all its puffing and noise.

The ending, sadly, was less glorious. A few days later the engine broke down while out on the road. The story goes that Trevithick and his friends pushed it into a shelter and went off to an inn for a meal and something to drink, perhaps a Christmas roast goose, leaving the fire still burning under the boiler. With nobody watching, the water in the boiler boiled away. The empty boiler grew red hot, and the fire spread to the wooden parts of the machine and the building around it. By the time anyone came back, the Puffing Devil was a burned-out wreck.

Trevithick blamed careless operating, not his design, and he was right that a dry boiler is a disaster. But it was a lesson he never forgot. Today the Trevithick Society has built a working replica of the Puffing Devil, which has been driven through Camborne on Trevithick Day, a festival held in the town in his honour.

sections.heading: London Streets and an Explosion at Greenwich
paragraphs: Trevithick did not give up on road vehicles. In 1803 he and Vivian built a new machine, often called the London Steam Carriage, which looked like a tall stagecoach body perched above a steam engine and huge rear wheels. It was driven through the streets of London, carrying passengers, and it worked. But the roads were rough and full of horses, carts and people, the carriage was expensive to run, and nobody wanted to buy it. In the end the engine was sold off to power a mill. Road steam had to wait.

Around the same time, Trevithick's engines were being built elsewhere. In 1802, the Coalbrookdale Company in Shropshire, famous ironmakers, built a high-pressure engine for him, and a drawing survives of what seems to be a small rail locomotive built there. We know very little about it. It may have been tested, or it may never have run at all, so historians are careful not to claim it as the first.

Then, in 1803, came a disaster that gave Trevithick's critics just what they wanted. One of his high-pressure engines, used to pump water at Greenwich near London, exploded, killing four men. According to Trevithick's side of the story, the engine had been left in the care of an inexperienced worker, and the safety valve had been fastened down so that it could not open, so the pressure built up until the boiler burst. Boulton and Watt seized on the accident as proof that high-pressure steam was deadly.

Trevithick argued that the engine had been badly handled, not badly designed. But he took the danger seriously. On later engines he fitted two safety valves, so that if one stuck, the other would still let steam out. He also added a clever device called a fusible plug: a plug of lead set into the boiler just above the fire. If the water level fell too low, the lead would heat up and melt, letting steam rush out and put the fire out before the boiler could become dangerously overheated. Ideas like these made high-pressure steam much safer, and versions of them were used on steam locomotives for well over a century.

sections.heading: The Great Bet at Penydarren
paragraphs: Now our story moves to South Wales, to Merthyr Tydfil, which around 1800 was becoming one of the greatest iron-making towns in the world. Its valleys were full of blast furnaces belonging to rival ironmasters. One of them was Samuel Homfray, owner of the Penydarren ironworks. Homfray was interested in Trevithick's high-pressure engines and in 1803 he brought Trevithick to Penydarren to build engines for the works.

Merthyr at that time was a noisy, smoky, booming place. Four huge ironworks, Cyfarthfa, Dowlais, Plymouth and Penydarren, crowded into the valley, their furnaces glowing day and night and lighting up the sky. Thousands of workers had poured in from the Welsh countryside, from England and from Ireland to dig coal and iron ore and to work the furnaces. The ironmasters were fiercely competitive, always looking for an advantage over each other, which helps explain why one of them was willing to gamble on a brand-new machine.

The ironmasters of Merthyr shared a tramroad, a horse-drawn plateway made of L-shaped cast-iron plates, which carried their iron down the valley to the canal wharf at Abercynon. There the iron was loaded onto boats on the Glamorganshire Canal and taken to the port of Cardiff. The tramroad was just under 10 miles (about 16 km) long, and horses pulled wagons along it every day.

Homfray had a bold idea. Could Trevithick's engine be put on wheels and made to pull the wagons instead of horses? Another ironmaster, Richard Crawshay of the Cyfarthfa ironworks, thought the idea was nonsense. So the two men made a bet. Each put up 500 guineas, a huge sum of money at the time, enough to buy a fine house, and handed it to a third ironmaster, Richard Hill of the Plymouth ironworks, to hold. Homfray would win if a steam engine could haul 10 tons of iron along the tramroad to Abercynon and bring the empty wagons back.

Trevithick began work in the autumn of 1803 and had his locomotive ready by February 1804. It looked very different from the trains you know. It had a single large horizontal cylinder set into a round iron boiler, a long piston rod sticking out in front, and a big flywheel at the side to keep the motion smooth. Gears carried the power to the four wheels, which ran on the plates of the tramroad. A fireman fed the fire, and the chimney rose from the same end of the boiler as the fire door, because the hot gases travelled along a U-shaped tube through the water and back again, giving them more time to heat it.

On 21 February 1804, the moment came. Behind the engine were five wagons carrying about 10 tons of iron. And then, as word spread, around 70 men climbed aboard the wagons for the ride, adding several more tons. With a great puffing and clanking, the locomotive set off down the valley from Penydarren towards Abercynon, nearly 10 miles away.

It was not a smooth trip. In places the crew had to stop to cut down overhanging branches and move rocks out of the way. Even so, the engine kept going. The whole journey took a little over four hours, which works out at an average of only a couple of miles per hour, though on good stretches it went faster, reaching around 5 miles per hour. Trevithick wrote proudly to his friend Davies Giddy that the engine had worked well and that no water was added to the boiler during the trip. According to accounts of the run, the engine burned only about two hundredweight of coal on the way down, roughly 100 kilograms, a surprisingly small pile for such a heavy load. Compare that with the horses it was meant to replace: a single horse could pull perhaps a couple of tons on the tramroad, so moving 10 tons of iron plus 70 passengers in one go would have needed a whole team of animals and several trips.

Trevithick also noticed something important. The used steam from the cylinder went up the chimney, and each puff seemed to make the fire burn more fiercely, pulling air through it. He commented on this effect in his letters. It was the same principle as the blastpipe that, as we will see in Part 7, would later help Rocket win its famous trial.

Whether Homfray actually won the bet is still unclear. On the way back up the valley, a bolt sheared and the boiler leaked, so the crew had to drop the fire, and the engine did not get back to Penydarren until the next day. Crawshay argued that the terms had not been met, and nobody knows for sure if the 500 guineas were ever paid. But in the history books, 21 February 1804 is remembered as the day when, for the first known time anywhere in the world, a steam locomotive hauled a load along rails.

sections.heading: Too Heavy for the Track
paragraphs: There was one big problem, and it was not the engine. It was the track. The Penydarren locomotive weighed around 5 tons, far more than a loaded horse wagon. The tramroad's plates were made of cast iron, which is hard but brittle, like a biscuit. It can hold a steady weight well, but sudden knocks and heavy pounding make it snap. As the locomotive rumbled along, the plates cracked and broke under its wheels.

After a few more trips, the ironworks decided the engine was causing more damage than it was worth. The wheels were taken off, and the engine was put to work standing still, driving machinery at the ironworks, including a forge hammer. Horses went back to pulling the wagons along the tramroad.

In 1981, the National Museum of Wales built a full-size, working reconstruction of the Penydarren locomotive, based on the evidence that survives. When it was run on a short track, it too broke the rails, a perfect demonstration of Trevithick's problem nearly 180 years later. The replica has been steamed each year at the National Waterfront Museum in Swansea, where visitors can see and hear it in action.

Trevithick tried again in the north of England. In 1804 and 1805, a locomotive to his design was built at Gateshead, on the River Tyne, by his agent John Whitfield, for Christopher Blackett, the owner of Wylam Colliery. It may have been the first locomotive with flanged wheels, designed to run on edge rails rather than plates. But Wylam's track was made of wood, and once again the engine was far too heavy for it. Blackett never used it on his wagonway, and it ended up as a stationary engine. Still, the people of Wylam had seen what a locomotive could be, and as Part 5 will show, they would not forget.

sections.heading: Catch Me Who Can
paragraphs: In 1808 Trevithick decided to show off his invention to the people of London, the biggest and richest city in Britain. He had a new locomotive built by the engineers John Hazledine and John Urpeth Rastrick at their foundry in Bridgnorth, Shropshire. It weighed about 8 tons, and it had a cheeky name: 'Catch Me Who Can'.

Trevithick set up what was called a 'steam circus' on open ground in Bloomsbury, close to where Euston Square is today. Land here is now covered by buildings of University College London. He laid a circular track about 100 feet (around 30 metres) across and surrounded it with a tall wooden fence, so that people had to pay to come in. Trial runs began in July 1808. For one shilling, visitors could watch the engine running round and round, or even ride in an open carriage pulled behind it.

Imagine the scene: Londoners in top hats and long dresses paying their shilling, stepping through the gate, and climbing into a carriage behind a hissing iron machine. Then, with a puff and a jolt, they are off, rattling around the ring faster than many of them had ever travelled. Reports say the engine reached about 12 miles per hour on the tight circle, and Trevithick believed it could manage 20 miles per hour on a straight track. A ticket card from the circus survives, with a picture of the engine and the slogan 'Mechanical Power Subduing Animal Speed'.

Sadly, the circus was a short-lived show. The ground was soft, and the iron rails kept breaking under the heavy engine. Trevithick replaced them with thick timber beams, but within about two months a broken rail caused the engine to come off the track. Visitor numbers had been disappointing anyway, and Trevithick could not afford to repair everything. The steam circus closed. Catch Me Who Can was the last railway locomotive he ever designed.

sections.heading: Why the Pioneer Never Got Rich
paragraphs: You might expect the man who built the world's first railway locomotive to have become rich and famous. Trevithick did not. Part of the reason was the track: until rails strong enough for heavy engines were made, his locomotives broke more than they saved. Part of it was his own restless character. He was full of ideas, but once he had shown that something could be done, he often lost interest and rushed on to the next project, without the patient business sense needed to make money from it.

And there were plenty of other projects. From 1805 he worked on a tunnel under the River Thames at Rotherhithe, digging a small trial passage beneath the river. In December 1807 and January 1808 the river burst in, and Trevithick nearly drowned. The project was abandoned. He designed steam dredgers to clear rivers, iron tanks for storing water on ships, and even engines for boats. In 1810 he fell seriously ill with typhoid, and in February 1811 he and his business partner Robert Dickinson were declared bankrupt.

Then came the greatest adventure of all. Silver mines high in the Andes mountains of Peru, around Cerro de Pasco, were flooded, and their owners wanted Trevithick's compact high-pressure engines to pump them out. In October 1816 he sailed from Penzance to South America, hoping to make his fortune. For a while it seemed he might. But wars of independence were sweeping the continent, and mines and machinery were wrecked in the fighting. Trevithick even served for a time with the army of the revolutionary leader Simón Bolívar. He later explored for minerals in Costa Rica and struggled through jungles and rivers in search of a route home.

In 1827, in the port of Cartagena in what is now Colombia, penniless and exhausted, Trevithick met by chance another British engineer: Robert Stephenson, the young son of George Stephenson, who was on his way home from mining work in South America. Robert Stephenson gave Trevithick 50 pounds to pay for his passage. Trevithick arrived in Falmouth, Cornwall, in October 1827 with almost nothing but the clothes he wore. He had been away for eleven years.

He spent his last years still inventing, and asking the government for a reward for his work, without success. He died of pneumonia on 22 April 1833 at the Bull Inn in Dartford, Kent, where he had been working on a new engine. He had no money, and no family were at his bedside. Workers from the local engineering works where he had been employed paid for his funeral and carried his coffin. He was buried in an unmarked grave in Dartford, where a plaque now remembers him.

Today Trevithick is far better remembered. A bronze statue of him stands in Camborne, holding a model of his engine. Merthyr Tydfil has a monument to the 1804 journey. A memorial window in Westminster Abbey honours him. And every year Camborne celebrates Trevithick Day with steam engines puffing through the streets. Railway historians agree that, whatever came later, Richard Trevithick built the first locomotive to run on rails.

sections.heading: Proof That It Could Be Done
paragraphs: Let us count up what Trevithick achieved between 1801 and 1808. He proved that a high-pressure steam engine could be made light and strong enough to move itself. He proved that it could carry people up a steep hill, and pull 10 tons of iron and 70 men along a track. He worked out safety devices to tame dangerous high-pressure boilers. He noticed how exhaust steam could fan the fire. And he showed thousands of Londoners that riding behind a steam engine was possible, and even fun.

What he had not done was make it work every day. His engines were too heavy for the brittle cast-iron plates and wooden rails of the time, and they were not yet reliable enough to replace horses year after year. Those were problems of track, grip, cost and patient improvement.

Trevithick had shown it could be done. Now, in the coalfields of northern England, around Leeds and Newcastle, colliery engineers with heavy loads to shift, plenty of cheap coal, and short tracks of their own were about to take his idea and make it work, day after day, in all weathers.

deepDive: Historians agree that the Penydarren locomotive of 21 February 1804 is the first steam locomotive known for certain to have hauled a load on rails, but the details reward careful reading. Different sources give the distance as about 9 to 9.75 miles and the time as roughly four hours, which implies an average of only about 2.4 mph; higher figures of close to 5 mph refer to the engine's speed on good stretches, not the whole trip, which included stops to clear the line. The Coalbrookdale engine of 1802 complicates the 'first' question: a drawing and a letter suggest a small locomotive was built, but there is no firm evidence it ever ran, so most historians credit Penydarren. Equally debated is why Trevithick's breakthrough did not catch on immediately. The usual answer is the track. His engines weighed about 5 to 8 tons, while cast-iron plateways had been designed for horse wagons of a few tons, and cast iron is strong when squeezed but weak when bent or struck. Only when stronger rails appeared, especially rolled wrought-iron rails from 1820, did heavy locomotives become practical. A second factor is economics. During the Napoleonic Wars horse fodder became very expensive, which later made locomotives attractive to colliery owners; in 1804 horses were still cheap enough. Third, Trevithick's own business choices mattered: he patented his high-pressure engine in 1802 but did not build a business around locomotives, preferring new challenges. Some historians also stress his contribution to stationary power, arguing that his high-pressure 'Cornish' boiler and engine work were even more important to industry than his locomotives. Finally, there is the question of the blastpipe. Trevithick clearly noticed that exhaust steam sent up the chimney increased the draught, but whether he deliberately designed a blastpipe or simply observed the effect is still debated, and several engineers, including Timothy Hackworth and George Stephenson, later developed the idea further.
funFact: A replica of Trevithick's Penydarren locomotive built in 1981 cracked its rails just like the original did in 1804, proving that the problem really was the track and not the storytellers.
